subtype: Approach: mock interview with a mentor before the panel [Action]
passage:
Day 1, nine days before the panel. Aadhya's draft was neat: attended the weekly sync, wrote monthly reports, handled client tickets, supported two projects.

Day 3. She read it to her mentor Vikas over coffee. Vikas listened, then said, "You've told me what you did. I still don't know what changed because of it." Aadhya's cheeks went warm.

Day 6. She rewrote the whole page around results: cut monthly reporting from three days to one, which freed the analysts for project work, and brought in two client accounts.

Day 9. The panel asked follow-up questions about the results, not about her schedule.

qa.q: How long did monthly reporting take after Aadhya's change?
qa.a: Monthly reporting went from three days to one.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when the mentor said it was unclear what had changed?
qa.a: Aadhya felt embarrassed and stung, and her cheeks went warm, but the comment showed her what the panel would want.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya do before the panel, and why?
qa.a: Aadhya could ask Vikas to run one more mock round with tough questions, because practice answering out loud makes results easier to explain.

qa.q: How might the panel see the rewritten case?
qa.a: The panel probably finds it clearer and more convincing, since results and outcomes are easier to judge than a list of tasks.

grounding: Illustrates presenting a promotion case to a mentor before the panel, hearing that it lists tasks instead of impact, and rewriting it around results.

subtype: Approach: mock interview with a mentor before the panel [Action]
passage:
Zubin, you're nervous about your panel on Friday? Sit, let me tell you about mine, back when I, Alka, was twenty-five and working in a hotel group.
I had my slides ready. Nine of them, full of everything I'd done: rosters, audits, vendor meetings. I was proud.
My mentor then was Mrs. Kurien, the old front-office director. She said, "Show me as if I'm the panel." So I did, in her cabin, all nine slides.
She listened, then said, "Alka, you told me what you did. You didn't tell me what changed because you did it."
I was hurt. I'd worked so hard on those slides. But that night I went through each one. The rosters meant overtime costs fell. The audits meant guest complaints dropped. I rewrote everything around results.
The panel asked me three questions, all about outcomes. I had answers.

qa.q: How many slides did Alka prepare at first?
How did Alka feel on hearing Mrs. Kurien's feedback?
qa.a: Alka felt hurt, having worked hard and felt proud of the slides.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Alka's story, and what did Alka choose there?
qa.a: The turning point was Mrs. Kurien's line about what changed; Alka chose to rewrite every slide around results that night instead of defending the list of tasks.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Kurien have felt watching the first version?
qa.a: Mrs. Kurien may have been caring but concerned, seeing a hardworking person about to undersell the work in front of the panel.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling a mock presentation to a mentor who pointed out a list of tasks instead of impact, and the rewrite around results that followed.

subtype: Approach: mock interview with a mentor before the panel [Action]
passage:
Pooja's promotion panel was at nine the next morning, and her mentor Chinmay could only spare the twenty-minute cab ride to the airport.
She sat in the back seat with her laptop on her knees and presented anyway, over the noise of honking on the Outer Ring Road.
"I led the vendor migration, ran six workshops, wrote the new process guide, handled the audit..."
Chinmay held up a hand. "Stop. That's a to-do list. What happened because of the migration?"
"Invoice errors dropped a lot. And payments went out faster."
"Then say that. The panel is paying for outcomes."
The cab pulled up at Departures. He jumped out. "Results first, tasks second."
Pooja rode back alone, rewriting in her notes app. By midnight each slide began with a result: fewer errors, faster payments, fewer audit issues.
She was annoyed at herself, then oddly calm.

qa.q: How long was the cab ride?
How did Pooja feel after rewriting the slides?
qa.a: She was annoyed at herself for listing tasks, then oddly calm once each slide began with a result.

qa.q: What else could Pooja do if there was no time to practise with Chinmay again?
qa.a: She could present the rewritten version aloud to a friend or record herself, checking that each point starts with an outcome.

qa.q: How does the mock pitch look from Chinmay's side?
qa.a: With only twenty minutes, Chinmay sees quickly that the pitch lists tasks, so the most useful thing is one sharp correction rather than detailed notes.

grounding: It shows someone presenting a promotion case to a mentor under time pressure, hearing that it lists tasks, and rewriting it around results.
